newsitem.title: New Zealand: NZ's Clark says evidence deal may double TV price.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Clark says evidence deal may double TV price.

text.p: An executive of Maori television station Aotearoa Television has told the opposition Labour Party the price it paid for equipment and facilities from 601 Digital was to double if it won extra government funding from February 6, Labour leader Helen Clark said on Friday.
She called for an urgent meeting of ministers because it appeared the government was not appropriating taxpayers' money for a proper purpose by providing $4 million in extra funding for Aotearoa.
On Monday, cabinet agreed to provide $4 million to keep the television network on air until June. The company produces Maori language television programmes for an Auckland audience.

Labour MP Trevor Mallard met Aotearoa chief executive Puhi Rangiaho on Friday but could not examine all the documentation about the finances of the station because it was in the hands of financial controller Derek Burns, Clark said in a statement.
Clark said Rangiaho had made the "startling revelation" to Mallard.
"If Ms Rangiaho is correct, this makes the government's claim that the further funding was purchasing only Maori programming complete nonsense," Clark said.
"The price the government was paying from February 6 to the end of June apparently enabled the vendors of 601 Digital to double the price of what they were selling."

She said Burns, a director of Aotearoa, appeared to have been on both ends of the transaction and would appear to gain directly from an extra $1.2 million that goes to 601 Digital if Ms Rangiaho is correct.

The Independent Business Weekly reported a company asssociated with Burns bought the assets of 601 Digital for $813,000 and on-sold them soon after for $2.3 million to Maori television station Aotearoa.

Earlier Martin Lekner, director of property company Terra Firma, told Reuters the company's Auckland studios leased to 601 Digital may have been sub-sub-leased to Aotearoa without the required approval.
Property industry sources told Reuters the property was leased to 601 Digital for about $300,000 a year for four years in December.

New Zealand's Serious Fraud Office said on Thursday it had launched a preliminary inquiry into the Aotearoa Television Network and there are other investigations by Commerce Ministry officials and private contacts of Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters.

Peters initiated his inquiries after revelations of links between the company and two men at the centre of the "Winebox" tax inquiry into use of the Cook Islands as a tax haven by New Zealand corporates in the 1980s.
